Is the House Hack Dead? Can a Rental Property Still Pay for Itself in 2026?

Look beyond the rent-versus-mortgage comparison. A practical perspective on duplexes, casitas and the full cost of ownership.

By Reddy Appraisal LLCOctober 21, 20263 min read

IN THIS ARTICLE

Why the numbers need a closer lookEvaluate the whole property, not just the mortgageChoose a goal and stress-test your assumptionsMore in Investment & Business ↗← All 24 articles

THE SHORT ANSWER

House hacking isn't dead; the easy assumptions are. Start with a clear goal: reduce your own housing payment, build long-term equity, or generate monthly cash flow. Compare properties on the same after-expense basis.

Why the numbers need a closer look

Remember when house hacking sounded almost too easy? Buy a duplex, live in one unit, rent the other, and let your tenant help pay the mortgage. Or rent out a spare room or a permitted backyard casita. The idea still has appeal, especially in Tucson, where different property layouts can create interesting opportunities. But with average 30-year mortgage rates at 7.40% as of October 15, 2026, plus rising ownership expenses, the math is less forgiving. A property that looked like a winner at a much lower rate might now barely break even.

Evaluate the whole property, not just the mortgage

The secret is to underwrite the whole property, not just compare rent with the mortgage. Add property taxes, insurance, utilities, repairs, vacancy, capital improvements, and a reserve for surprises. If you're considering a short-term rental, tools such as AirROI can help you research estimated revenue, occupancy, and seasonality. But treat those figures as a starting point, not a promise. Check local short-term rental rules, HOA restrictions, and whether the unit can legally be rented. Most importantly, run a conservative scenario: what happens if rent is lower than expected or the property sits vacant for two months?

Choose a goal and stress-test your assumptions

House hacking isn't dead; the easy assumptions are. Start with a clear goal: reduce your own housing payment, build long-term equity, or generate monthly cash flow. Compare a duplex, a home with a legal accessory dwelling unit, and a traditional single-family rental on the same after-expense basis. Keep cash reserves, understand your financing terms, and have a backup plan if short-term rental demand weakens. Before you buy, make sure the purchase price is supported by the market. The smartest house hack isn't the one with the flashiest revenue projection - it's the one that still makes sense when reality is less exciting than the spreadsheet.
